---
title: "13. Sample size and power"
format: html
---

**Slides covered.** `BIOS-767-Part-022.pdf`, slides 4-23.

## Motivation and target

Consider a two-group longitudinal study testing whether linear rates of change differ. Let $N_1=\pi N$, $N_0=(1-\pi)N$, and

$$
\delta=\beta_1^{(1)}-\beta_1^{(0)}.
$$

Here $N$ is the required total number of participants across both groups—not the number per group—with $N_1$ assigned to group 1 and $N_0$ assigned to group 0. This is the required sample size before inflation for expected dropout or nonadherence.

The null is $H_0:\delta=0$ against a two-sided alternative.

## Planning model

For subject $i$ at common times $t_1,\ldots,t_n$,

$$
Y_{ij}=(\beta_0^{(z_i)}+b_{0i})
+(\beta_1^{(z_i)}+b_{1i})t_j+\varepsilon_{ij},
$$

with

$$
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0i}\\b_{1i}\end{pmatrix}
\sim N\!\left[
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}d_{00}&d_{01}\\d_{01}&d_{11}\end{pmatrix}
\right],
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma_e^2).
$$

The variance of a subject-specific OLS slope is

$$
\sigma_\beta^2
=\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_{1i})
=d_{11}+
\frac{\sigma_e^2}{\sum_{j=1}^n(t_j-\bar t)^2},
\qquad
\bar t=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^nt_j.
$$

*Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-022.pdf`, slides 5-9.*

## Planned inference and closed-form sample size

Under equal slope variance in both groups,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\delta)
=\sigma_\beta^2\left(\frac1{N_1}+\frac1{N_0}\right)
=\frac{\sigma_\beta^2}{N\pi(1-\pi)}.
$$

The normal-approximation test rejects $H_0:\delta=0$ when

$$
\left|\frac{\widehat\delta}
{\sigma_\beta/\sqrt{N\pi(1-\pi)}}\right|
>z_{1-\alpha/2}.
$$

Using the normal approximation to a two-sample slope comparison,

$$
N=
\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\gamma})^2\sigma_\beta^2}
{\pi(1-\pi)\delta^2},
$$

where $1-\gamma$ is power. Round upward and inflate for expected dropout/nonadherence. Balanced allocation $\pi=1/2$ minimizes $N$ when per-subject costs and variances are equal. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-022.pdf`, slides 9-10. The slides state the result; proof is omitted.*

The formula shows:

$$
N\propto \sigma_\beta^2,\qquad
N\propto\delta^{-2},\qquad
N\propto\{\pi(1-\pi)\}^{-1}.
$$

More widely spread measurement times reduce the residual contribution through $\sum_j(t_j-\bar t)^2$, but cannot reduce the irreducible random-slope variance $d_{11}$.

## Simulation-based power

Use simulation when the analysis includes nonlinear time, GLMM/GEE estimation, irregular schedules, complex covariance, small-sample degrees of freedom, missingness, nonconvergence, or multiplicity:

1. Specify design, parameters, covariance/random effects, and observation process.
2. Generate complete outcomes under a scientifically justified alternative.
3. Generate missingness and protocol deviations.
4. Apply the exact planned analysis, including model selection only if it will occur in practice.
5. Record rejection, bias, coverage, convergence, and usable sample size.
6. Estimate power by

   $$
   \widehat{\mathrm{Power}}=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^BI(p_b<\alpha),
   \qquad
   \operatorname{MCSE}=
   \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Power}}(1-\widehat{\mathrm{Power}})}{B}}.
   $$

Here $p_b$ is the p-value from applying the planned hypothesis test to simulated dataset $b$. The Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) measures the simulation uncertainty in $\widehat{\mathrm{Power}}$ from using a finite number $B$ of simulated datasets.

*Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-022.pdf`, slides 11-23.*

## Missingness sensitivity

Under MNAR, a simple attrition inflation is insufficient because both effective information and estimand bias can change. Simulate several observation models, including outcome-dependent dropout, and evaluate bias and type-I error in addition to power. *Slide source: `BIOS-767-Part-022.pdf`, slides 18-23.*

## Interpretation and when to apply

Use the closed form for a common-time, Gaussian linear-slope design under the stated random-intercept/slope model. Use simulation for the final design whenever the planned analysis departs materially from those assumptions. Planning values for $d_{11}$, $\sigma_e^2$, and $\delta$ should come from external/pilot evidence and be varied over plausible ranges.
